","char_count":942,"fact_ids":[],"source_anchors":[]},{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":3,"domain":"Illinois signals markings railroads","heading":"C — signals markings railroads","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Illinois signals markings railroads

FACT_ID: sec14-F01 | anchor: A01
Obey signals and roadway markings unless a police or traffic-control officer directs otherwise, and never leave the road to evade a signal. [A01]
Why it matters: group Signal authority; recall cue Officer direction can override signal.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F02 | anchor: A01
A typical three-color traffic signal orders red, yellow and green from top to bottom or left to right. [A01]
Why it matters: group Signal layout; recall cue Red, yellow, green in standard sequence.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F03 | anchor: A01
A nonworking intersection signal requires an all-way stop, then observation and yielding before entry, unless police direct another action. [A01]
Why it matters: group Failed signals; recall cue Dark signal becomes all-way stop.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F04 | anchor: A01
At a red signal, stop before the marked line, otherwise before the crosswalk or intersection, and wait for green and a clear intersection unless making a permitted red-light turn. [A01]
Why it matters: group Steady red; recall cue Red requires stop at proper location.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F05 | anchor: A01
After a full stop and yielding to pedestrians and approaching traffic, a right turn on red is allowed unless a sign prohibits it. [A01]
Why it matters: group Red-light turns; recall cue Right on red requires stop, yield and permission.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F06 | anchor: A01
A left turn on red is allowed from a one-way street onto a one-way street carrying traffic leftward after stopping and yielding. [A01]
Why it matters: group Red-light turns; recall cue One-way left on red has specific route.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F07 | anchor: A01
A steady yellow warns that green is changing to red, and the driver must not enter once red appears. [A01]
Why it matters: group Steady yellow; recall cue Yellow announces ending green.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F08 | anchor: A01
A green signal permits movement only after yielding to vehicles and pedestrians already in the crossing or intersection. [A01]
Why it matters: group Steady green; recall cue Green still yields to occupied crossing.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F09 | anchor: A01
At a flashing red intersection signal, stop, yield to traffic in the intersection or crosswalk and proceed only when safe. [A01]
Why it matters: group Flashing signals; recall cue Flashing red follows stop-and-yield rule.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F10 | anchor: A01
A flashing yellow intersection light allows proceeding cautiously. [A01]
Why it matters: group Flashing signals; recall cue Flashing yellow means caution.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec14-F11 | anchor: A02
Movement in a traffic arrow’s direction still requires yielding to traffic and pedestrians already in the intersection or crosswalk. [A02]
Why it matters: group Arrow signals; recall cue Arrow direction still respects occupied crossing.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F12 | anchor: A02
A steady red arrow generally forbids its indicated movement, but the handbook allows a right turn or the stated one-way-to-one-way left turn after a full stop and yielding. [A02]
Why it matters: group Arrow signals; recall cue Red-arrow exceptions require stopping and yielding.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F13 | anchor: A02
A steady yellow arrow warns that a green arrow is ending or that the signal will soon turn red. [A02]
Why it matters: group Arrow signals; recall cue Steady yellow arrow ends protected interval.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F14 | anchor: A02
A flashing yellow arrow allows a turn in its direction after yielding to vehicles and pedestrians in the intersection or crosswalk. [A02]
Why it matters: group Arrow signals; recall cue Flashing yellow arrow permits yielded turn.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F15 | anchor: A02
A green arrow pointing up allows straight travel only, while a right- or left-pointing arrow permits the indicated turn. [A02]
Why it matters: group Arrow signals; recall cue Green arrow limits movement to shown direction.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F16 | anchor: A02
A pedestrian facing a walking-person signal may cross in the signal’s direction. [A02]
Why it matters: group Pedestrian signals; recall cue Walking-person signal permits directed crossing.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F17 | anchor: A02
A flashing orange raised hand means do not begin crossing, but someone who began under a steady walking signal may finish to the sidewalk or safety island. [A02]
Why it matters: group Pedestrian signals; recall cue Flashing hand does not stop an already-started crossing.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F18 | anchor: A02
A steady orange raised hand means do not enter the roadway. [A02]
Why it matters: group Pedestrian signals; recall cue Steady hand means no new entry.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F19 | anchor: A02
An overhead red cross means the lane cannot be used. [A02]
Why it matters: group Lane signals; recall cue Red lane cross closes lane.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F20 | anchor: A02
An overhead yellow cross warns of a coming red cross, so leave the lane safely before it turns red. [A02]
Why it matters: group Lane signals; recall cue Yellow lane cross requires safe exit.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F21 | anchor: A02
The handbook’s flashing yellow overhead arrow identifies a lane available for approaching and making a left turn. [A02]
Why it matters: group Lane signals; recall cue Flashing yellow lane indication serves left turns.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F22 | anchor: A02
A green lane arrow permits lane use subject to all other traffic signs and signals. [A02]
Why it matters: group Lane signals; recall cue Green lane arrow does not override other controls.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec14-F23 | anchor: A03
A solid white edge line marks the road’s right boundary, while a solid yellow line marks the left edge of a divided roadway. [A03]
Why it matters: group Edge lines; recall cue Edge-line color distinguishes road side.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-F24 | anchor: A03
White lane lines divide lanes traveling in the same direction. [A03]
Why it matters: group White lane lines; recall cue White separates same-direction traffic.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R01 | anchor: A01
A broken white line may be crossed to change lanes or turn. [A01]
Why it matters: group White lane lines; recall cue Broken white permits specified crossing.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R02 | anchor: A01
Crossing a single solid white lane line is discouraged and requires special caution. [A01]
Why it matters: group White lane lines; recall cue Single solid white discourages crossing.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R03 | anchor: A01
Crossing a double solid white lane boundary is prohibited. [A01]
Why it matters: group White lane lines; recall cue Double solid white prohibits crossing.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R04 | anchor: A01
Yellow center markings separate traffic moving in opposite directions. [A01]
Why it matters: group Yellow center lines; recall cue Yellow separates opposing traffic.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R05 | anchor: A01
A broken yellow center line allows passing between opposing single lanes when the maneuver is otherwise safe and lawful. [A01]
Why it matters: group Yellow center lines; recall cue Broken yellow permits passing subject to other rules.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R06 | anchor: A01
Double solid yellow center lines may be crossed for a left turn into or out of an alley, private road, driveway or street. [A01]
Why it matters: group Yellow center lines; recall cue Double yellow has left-access-turn exception.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R07 | anchor: A01
A solid yellow line on your side marks a no-passing area, but it may be crossed to finish a pass begun before the area or to make the stated left-access turn. [A01]
Why it matters: group Yellow no-passing lines; recall cue No-passing line retains stated completion and turn exceptions.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec14-R08 | anchor: A02
With one broken and one solid yellow center line, passing is allowed only from the side nearest the broken line. [A02]
Why it matters: group Yellow center lines; recall cue Broken-line side determines passing permission.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R09 | anchor: A02
A two-way left-turn lane is identified by yellow lines and white arrows, and left turns must use that lane when it is provided. [A02]
Why it matters: group Shared turn lanes; recall cue Provided center turn lane is required for left turn.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R10 | anchor: A02
Use a two-way left-turn lane only to prepare for or make a left turn into or out of the road, or a lawful U-turn. [A02]
Why it matters: group Shared turn lanes; recall cue Shared center lane is not a through lane.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R11 | anchor: A02
A white transverse stop line marks where a red light or stop sign requires stopping, with every part of the vehicle remaining behind the line. [A02]
Why it matters: group Stop lines; recall cue Whole vehicle stops before white line.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R12 | anchor: A02
In urban areas the stop line is usually four feet before the crosswalk. [A02]
Why it matters: group Stop lines; recall cue Stop line generally precedes urban crosswalk.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R13 | anchor: A02
White crosswalk markings span the pavement and can include diagonal stripes, and pedestrians in the crossing have priority over vehicles. [A02]
Why it matters: group Crosswalk markings; recall cue White crossing markings identify pedestrian priority.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R14 | anchor: A02
A marked crossing can be in the middle of a block and have a pedestrian-crossing sign at its white lines. [A02]
Why it matters: group Crosswalk markings; recall cue Crosswalk need not be at intersection.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R15 | anchor: A02
Diagonal yellow or white stripes mark fixed obstructions, and solid white or yellow lines can guide traffic around a hazard. [A02]
Why it matters: group Other pavement markings; recall cue Special markings identify and route around obstruction.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R16 | anchor: A02
Local authorities may designate no-parking areas using curb, fire-lane or pavement markings. [A02]
Why it matters: group Other pavement markings; recall cue No-parking control can be painted.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec14-R17 | anchor: A03
A round yellow advance railway warning with black crossed marks and railway letters may be placed up to seven hundred fifty feet before the tracks. [A03]
Why it matters: group Railway warnings; recall cue Round advance sign warns before crossing.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec14-R18 | anchor: A03
A solid yellow line before a railway crossing prohibits passing, and white stop lines indicate where to stop for a train. [A03]
Why it matters: group Railway markings; recall cue Rail markings separate passing and stopping duties.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec14-R19 | anchor: A03
A crossbuck functions as a yield control requiring priority for approaching rail traffic; a supplementary sign gives the number of tracks at a multiple-track crossing. [A03]
Why it matters: group Railway crossbucks; recall cue Crossbuck yields to trains and may show track count.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec14-R20 | anchor: A03
When railway warning lights flash, stop and stay stopped until the train passes and the flashing ends. [A03]
Why it matters: group Railway lights; recall cue Train passing alone does not release flashing-light stop.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec14-R21 | anchor: A03
Remain stopped until crossing gates are raised and warning lights stop flashing, and never drive around lowered gates or try to beat gates being lowered. [A03]
Why it matters: group Railway gates; recall cue Raised gates and stopped flashing are both required.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec14-R22 | anchor: A03
Automated crossing enforcement can record the plate, location and time of a violation, which can bring fines and possible license suspension. [A03]
Why it matters: group Railway enforcement; recall cue Crossing violation can be recorded automatically.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec14-R23 | anchor: A03
An emergency-notification sign identifies the railroad’s contact information and the specific crossing so the public can report an emergency to the responsible railroad. [A03]
Why it matters: group Railway emergency signs; recall cue Emergency sign identifies railroad and crossing.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]
